text: Alexander Henderson Manning (11 May 1819 – 20 October 1903) was a Canadian contractor, businessman, and the 20th Mayor of Toronto, serving a single term in 1873 and a second in 1885. Born in Dublin, Ireland, on 11 May 1819, he was educated there and immigrated to Toronto in 1834. Four years later, he lived in Ohio before returning to Toronto after two years. He worked as a builder and was a partner in a sawmill business. He worked on the construction of several projects, including the Welland Canal, the Library of Parliament, and the Toronto Normal and Model School. In the 1850s, he invested in real estate in Toronto. In the 1860s, he demanded overtime payments for road construction in Grey County, which was used to politically attack him for seeking excessive public funds. From 1870 to 1874, he worked on masonry and brickwork for the Canadian Library of Parliament. He was also an investor in the Toronto Street Railway and constructed railways in Vermont, Pennsylvania, New York, and other parts of Canada. Manning was unsuccessful in his first election as alderman for St. Lawrence Ward in 1855 but was elected in 1856 and reelected in 1857. He was not an alderman in the following council term but returned in 1867 and was reelected annually until 1873. He nominated himself for mayor in 1872 but was not selected by the city council; in 1873, he nominated himself again and was elected. During his first term, he advocated for a commissioner to oversee public projects and helped establish a system to assess and collect taxes. The city controversially purchased privately owned waterworks, which divided city council and the public. In 1874, he ran in the mayoral election that returned to popular vote but lost due to public allegations of misconduct in the waterworks tendering process. He won his first government contract to build the Welland Canal and Cornwall Canal. His 1879 contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway was criticized for being awarded due to his influence in the Conservative Party. A royal commission found the price was not rigged but noted irregularities in the awarding process, which damaged his ability to secure further contracts and led to his company going bankrupt in 1883. Manning ran for mayor in 1879 and came in third; he declined the nomination in 1881, but in 1884, over 5,000 citizens signed a petition for him to run. As an independent candidate, he focused on his prior experience as mayor, promising financial restraint and clean water. His opponent, John Jacob Withrow, criticized tax assessments on Manning’s income and businesses, and Manning responded by reading his assessor reports and defending the reductions he received. He won the mayoral race with support from Conservative voters. As mayor, he maintained low tax rates and was an effective city administrator. He advocated for a better sanitation system, though his reputation was hampered by associations with dishonest individuals. He also supported the creation of the Home for Incurables and called for the formation of the Toronto Volunteers Reception Committee to prepare for the return of troops from the North-West Rebellion, and formed a committee to build a monument to those who fought for the government in the rebellion, which was erected in 1895. Initially believing he would be unchallenged in his reelection, he faced a growing civic reform movement that produced candidate William Holmes Howland, a temperance advocate who highlighted Manning’s presidency of the Toronto Brewing and Malting Company. Manning supported the Daily Mail in its dispute with the Toronto Typographical Union, leading the union to campaign against him. He lost his reelection bid in 1885. Manning was active in several Toronto social organizations, including the Irish Protestant Benevolent Society, the St. Patrick's Society, and the National Club. He was an investor in the Grand Opera House and purchased it when it went bankrupt in 1876. In 1884, he hired E. J. Lennox to design the Manning Arcade and funded the construction of Old City Hall. He was a member of the Toronto Board of Trade, a director of the Traders Bank of Canada and the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and president of the Toronto Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company and the North American Land Company Limited. He married Adeline Augusta Whittemore on 6 February 1850; she died in 1861, and he married Susan Celina Smith on 1 August 1861. They had two sons and two daughters. Manning died in Toronto on 20 October 1903 and was buried at St. James Cemetery in a tomb he built for his family. At the time of his death, he was the largest individual taxpayer in Toronto.
